title: Accounting for Rising Corporate Profits: Intangibles or Regulatory Rents?
venue: Boston University School of Law, Law and Economics Research Paper No. 16-18 (SSRN working paper)
method: Firm-level decomposition of Tobin's Q and operating margins on R&D, organisational capital, lobbying, campaign spending and RegData regulation counts; difference-in-differences around major regulatory changes against matched control firms
finding: Capital investment and R&D explain much of the rise in valuations and profits in the 1990s, but political activity and regulation account for a surprisingly large share since 2000; firms experiencing major regulatory change see valuations rise about 12% relative to matched controls.
summary_plain: US company profits have risen since 1980. This study finds that since 2000 much of the rise is linked to regulation and lobbying, not only to innovation: firms hit by big new rules tended to become more valuable, not less.
relevance: Regulation can create rents for incumbents who can absorb compliance costs, so heavy EU digital rulebooks may entrench large platforms as well as constrain them.
caveats: US-only working paper, never published in a peer-reviewed journal; regulation counts are a crude proxy, and the DiD covers a limited set of major regulatory events.

authors: European Commission, Directorate-General for Competition (with OECD and Lear-led background studies)
title: Protecting competition in a changing world - Evidence on the evolution of competition in the EU during the past 25 years
venue: European Commission staff report (DG COMP), Publications Office of the EU, KD-09-24-494-EN-N
method: Descriptive industry-level CR4 concentration (Orbis) and firm-level markups (production-function approach), market-level sales data, plus OECD regressions linking concentration and markups to upstream regulatory burden and a macro model (MATER) simulation of markup effects on GDP
finding: Average firm markups across 23 European countries and 204 industries rose by 7% between 2000 and 2019, and average industry CR4 concentration rose by about 5 percentage points; a model simulation attributes a GDP loss of about 5.7% to the 7.54% markup increase if it fully reflects weaker competition. OECD regressions find industries relying on inputs from more heavily regulated sectors show higher concentration, but the report says the evidence is not sufficient to conclude with high certainty that rising regulatory barriers drove the trend.
summary_plain: The Commission's own review finds that competition in the EU has weakened over 25 years: big firms hold larger shares and charge higher margins. It says rules that raise the cost of doing business may help larger firms, but the evidence is not yet conclusive.
relevance: It is the Commission's own evidence base. It names regulatory barriers to entry as a possible cause of rising market power, and it cites the DMA as an example of pro-competitive regulation.
caveats: Mostly descriptive. Markup estimates depend on production-function assumptions, and the GDP figure is a model simulation that assumes the whole markup rise reflects lost competition.
interested_party: DG COMP is the EU competition enforcer and argues for stronger competition policy

title: The Theory of Economic Regulation
venue: The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 2(1): 3-21
geography_period: US (illustrative evidence on trucking weight limits and occupational licensing)
method: Political-economy theory of the supply and demand for regulation, with illustrative cross-state evidence
finding: As a rule, regulation is acquired by the industry and is designed and operated primarily for its benefit; concentrated producer interests outbid dispersed consumers for entry control, subsidies and price-fixing.
summary_plain: This classic paper argues that industries often seek regulation and shape it to protect themselves from competition. It is the origin of the idea of 'regulatory capture'.
relevance: It is the basic theory behind the worry that complex EU digital rules can be shaped by, and end up favouring, the large incumbents they are meant to discipline.
caveats: A theory with mostly illustrative evidence. Later work (Peltzman, Becker) shows that regulators also weigh consumer interests.

title: The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society
method: Theoretical model of competitive rent-seeking for import licences, with back-of-envelope estimates of rent values
finding: Rents created by government restrictions were estimated at about 7.3% of national income in India (1964), and import-licence rents alone at about 15% of GNP in Turkey (1968); competition for these rents wastes resources beyond the usual deadweight loss.
summary_plain: When governments hand out valuable permissions, firms spend real resources competing for them instead of producing. Krueger coined the term 'rent-seeking' and showed these rents can be large.
relevance: Licensing, designation and compliance regimes create valuable regulatory positions, and the effort spent lobbying for them is a cost of regulation in its own right.
caveats: Context is trade licensing in developing economies; the rent estimates are rough, and Krueger did not estimate how much of the rents were dissipated.

authors: Jan De Loecker; Jan Eeckhout; Gabriel Unger
title: The Rise of Market Power and the Macroeconomic Implications
method: Firm-level markups estimated with the production-function approach (output elasticity over cost share) from Compustat accounts
finding: Aggregate markups rose from 21% above marginal cost in 1980 to 61% by 2016, driven by the upper tail while the median is unchanged; the average profit rate rose from 1% to 8%.
summary_plain: Using company accounts, the authors find that US firms charge much higher prices relative to their costs than they did in 1980. The rise comes mostly from a small group of top firms.
relevance: This is the main benchmark for the 'rising market power' debate that EU digital competition policy, including the DMA, responds to.
caveats: Markup levels depend on the production-function assumptions and on treating overhead as a variable cost, and listed firms are not representative; others estimate smaller increases.

title: How European Markets Became Free: A Study of Institutional Drift (NBER WP 24700 revision titled 'How EU Markets Became More Competitive Than US Markets')
venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 21(1): 251-292 (NBER Working Paper 24700, 2018)
method: Political-economy model of national vs supranational regulators, tested with cross-country data on concentration, profits, product-market regulation and competition-authority independence
finding: European markets now have lower concentration, lower excess profits and lower regulatory barriers to entry than US markets; EU institutions are more independent and enforce competition more strongly than any individual country ever did, and countries with weaker institutions benefit most from delegation to the EU level.
summary_plain: Since the 1990s Europe's markets have become more open and competitive than America's. The authors credit independent EU-level competition enforcement and the deregulation of formerly protected sectors.
relevance: It suggests EU-level rules and enforcers can push against capture and incumbency, which is the main counterweight to the regulatory-rents view.
caveats: Evidence is largely cross-country and descriptive. Later revisions focus on telecoms and airlines, and the EC 2024 report finds EU concentration rising after 2000.

title: The Failure of Free Entry
method: Industry panel of entry rates on Tobin's Q; tests rival explanations (returns to scale, technology) against RegData regulation and lobbying expenditure, with an instrument-based analysis of regulation's effect by firm size
finding: The elasticity of entry with respect to Tobin's Q was positive and significant until the late 1990s but fell to zero afterwards; lobbying and regulations, not returns to scale or technology, explain the decline, and regulations reduce entry and growth of small firms relative to large ones, particularly in high-lobbying industries.
summary_plain: Profitable US industries used to attract new competitors, but since about 2000 they no longer do. The authors blame growing regulation and lobbying, which hurt small and new firms more than big ones.
relevance: It supports the view that regulation weighs most on small firms, which matters for the cumulative compliance load of EU digital law on start-ups and SMEs.
caveats: Working paper; US-only; regulation measured by RegData word counts. Goldschlag and Tabarrok find no link between regulation and declining dynamism.

title: The Great Reversal: How America Gave Up on Free Markets
venue: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press (book)
method: Book-length synthesis of the author's and others' research on concentration, profits, prices, lobbying and regulation
finding: US industries have become more concentrated and less competitive than European ones since the late 1990s, with higher prices (for example in mobile telecoms and airlines), lower investment and productivity; the author attributes this to lobbying and campaign finance that raised entry barriers and weakened antitrust.
summary_plain: Philippon argues that the US, once the model of free markets, now has less competition than Europe, and that lobbying by big firms is a main reason.
relevance: It is often cited for the claim that EU competition institutions have done better than US ones, and it frames lobbying-driven regulation as a risk.
caveats: Written for a general audience, so it argues a case; some claims (for example on prices and welfare) are disputed by other economists.

authors: Matias Covarrubias; Germán Gutiérrez; Thomas Philippon
title: From Good to Bad Concentration? US Industries over the Past 30 Years
method: Industry-level relationships among concentration, prices, investment, intangibles and leader productivity, split by period and initial concentration
finding: In the 1990s concentration was efficient, driven by tougher price competition, intangible investment and leaders' productivity; after 2000 it became inefficient, associated with lower investment, higher prices, lower productivity growth and rising barriers to entry.
summary_plain: Market concentration is not always bad. In the 1990s it reflected better firms winning; after 2000 it increasingly reflected entrenched leaders protected by barriers.
relevance: It warns against reading concentration in digital markets as automatically harmful or benign, and it points to barriers to entry (including regulatory ones) as the distinguishing factor.
caveats: Correlational industry evidence; classifying concentration as good or bad depends on proxies.

authors: Gábor Koltay; Szabolcs Lőrincz; Tommaso Valletti
title: Concentration and Competition: Evidence From Europe and Implications For Policy
method: Industry concentration (CR4, HHI) built from Orbis and Euromonitor data, plus aggregate profitability from national accounts
finding: Average industry concentration rose moderately over two decades, with a considerably larger share of high-concentration industries, a tendency toward oligopoly, and a sustained rise in aggregate profitability.
summary_plain: In Europe too, more industries are now dominated by a few large firms, and profits have risen, though less sharply than in the US.
relevance: It is Europe-specific evidence that market power is growing, and it feeds directly into the EC 2024 report and the case for ex-ante digital rules.
caveats: Descriptive; does not identify whether regulation or technology drives the trend; concentration measured at industry, not antitrust-market, level.
interested_party: Authors are (or were) DG COMP economists; Valletti is a former DG COMP Chief Economist

title: Regulatory Costs and Market Power
method: Machine learning on regulatory documents to measure industry compliance costs; panel regressions of firm outcomes on regulatory-cost shocks by firm size
finding: Regulatory costs rose by $1 trillion over 1970-2018; higher regulatory costs lower sales, employment, markups and profitability for small firms and raise them for large firms, and increased regulation can explain 31-37% of the rise in market power.
summary_plain: Compliance costs fall harder on small companies than big ones. This study estimates that growing US regulation explains about a third of the increase in big firms' market power since 1970.
relevance: It is direct evidence that compliance burdens can raise concentration, a key risk when many EU digital instruments apply to firms of all sizes.
caveats: Unpublished working paper; the cost measure comes from ML classification of regulatory text; US-only.

authors: Dustin Chambers; Patrick A. McLaughlin; Tyler Richards
title: Regulation, entrepreneurship, and firm size
geography_period: US industries (RegData 3.0 linked to Census SUSB data), late 1990s-2010s
method: Industry panel regressions of firm counts and employment by firm size on RegData industry-specific regulatory restriction counts, with industry and year fixed effects
finding: A 10% increase in industry-specific regulatory restrictions is associated with a 0.5% reduction in the number of firms and a 0.6% reduction in employment only among small firms; consecutive years of high regulatory growth amplify the negative effects for small firms but not large ones.
summary_plain: More rules in an industry go with fewer firms and fewer jobs at small businesses, while large firms are largely unaffected.
relevance: It uses restriction counts, the same kind of measure as this site's counts of legal restrictions, and links them to small-firm outcomes.
caveats: Associational; restriction word counts do not measure stringency; the 2018 working paper said only small-firm counts fell.
interested_party: Mercatus Center (George Mason University), a market-oriented think tank that built RegData

authors: Sara Calligaris; Chiara Criscuolo; Luca Marcolin
title: Mark-ups in the digital era
venue: OECD Science, Technology and Industry Working Papers, No. 2018/10
method: Firm-level markups estimated by the production-function approach on Orbis data, compared across sectors by digital intensity
finding: Average markups rose (about 8% over 2001-2014, as summarised in the EC 2024 report), driven by firms at the top of the distribution; digital-intensive sectors have higher markups than other sectors and the gap widened over time.
summary_plain: Across rich countries, firms' price margins rose in the 2000s, and the rise was greatest in sectors that use digital technology intensively.
relevance: It ties rising market power to digital-intensive sectors, the target of the DMA and related EU instruments.
caveats: Descriptive; the markup level depends on estimation assumptions; the 2024 update finds product-market regulation does not explain the digital markup gap.

title: Is regulation to blame for the decline in American entrepreneurship?
method: Industry panel linking Census business-dynamism measures (startup rates, job reallocation) to RegData federal regulation counts
finding: Rising federal regulation does not explain the long-run decline in US startup rates and job reallocation; the decline is broad-based across industries regardless of their regulatory growth.
summary_plain: This study finds no clear link between the growth of US federal rules and the long-run fall in new business creation.
relevance: It is contrary evidence: counts of regulation alone may not predict harm to entry, so cumulative-burden claims about EU digital law need careful testing.
caveats: RegData counts may miss stringency and uncertainty; covers federal rules only (not state licensing).
interested_party: Tabarrok is affiliated with the Mercatus Center (George Mason University), which built RegData
